title: The translation-memory API was declared as a full ModelViewSet, exposing unintended write endpoints without access control.

findings.explanation: The new MemoryViewSet.get_queryset gates the entire memory list (and the detail lookup used by destroy) on `self.request.user.is_superuser`. The project's documented permission model defines fine-grained `memory.edit` and `memory.delete` permissions (weblate/auth/data.py:59-61), and the existing web view (weblate/memory/views.py:50-58) authorizes memory access via `user.has_perm('memory.delete', ...)` / `user.has_perm('memory.edit')`, not superuser status. By using `is_superuser` instead of `has_perm`, the API grants access to superusers but denies it to any user who legitimately holds the `memory.delete`/`memory.edit` permission, and it bypasses the per-object ownership logic (a user may manage their own memory entries). This is an incorrect authorization check relative to the established access-control model.

Weblate comes with a fine-grained privilege system to assign user permissions for the whole instance, or in a limited scope.

findings.suggested_fix: Replace the `is_superuser` check in get_queryset with the same permission logic used by the web views: filter the queryset by the user's `memory.edit`/`memory.delete` permissions and ownership (e.g., allow entries where `user=request.user`, or where the user has the relevant global/project permission), mirroring weblate/memory/views.py check_perm rather than relying on superuser status.
